item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
You had me at "Animate fossils foraging." The incident report is pretty cool imagery, too. Bio stuff: you claim that it's a self sufficient environment - are there fossilized flora performing photosynthesis? Or fossilized microbes at the bottom of the food chain? Soft tissue doesn't tend to get fossilized.

Also, nitpicky: you use SCP-447 as synonymous with the entities in several cases ("SCP-477 are able to move"). I think that's incorrect in the formal format.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If the original writer wants some technical biology angle, I would be more than happy to provide. PM me. Leicontis also brings up some good questions below, which I'd also be happy to help answer.

In general, the more I ponder this thing, the more I like it. A few calculatedly-brief addenda regarding containment breaches could go a long way towards giving this a little more of a chilling edge, but even without it I rather like the idea. The imagery is delightful, and as Flames said, the idea of this thing getting loose is full of win.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Thanks.

I don't see a Euclid rating as being necessary simply because so far they aren't actually dangerous, just too weird to allow out into the world. That could change if:

Fossils might weaken the concrete, I hadn't considered that. Instead of including a lengthy Foundation test, I might just add a note in the incident report mentioning that the museum wall collapsed due to structural weakness once the fossils reached a critical concentration. I'll think about it.

I thought about the possibility of eggs or plankton surviving in pulverized debris, but it didn't seem an interesting enough detail to force readers to slog through a description of it. I could amend the containment procedures to include pulverizing rock, then converting it to an acidic slurry which would dissolve any fossilized material it still contained.

Good comments, thanks.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I had conceived of the layer of limestone being very thin, thin enough that organisms live at the "surface" and can't escape deeper into the rock because the way is blocked. I added a minor edit to help make that clear.

The bit about rock-adapted creatures can certainly go if it comes across as too silly. I only included it because, from an occam's razor standpoint, is it any sillier than animated fossils swimming through solid rock? It seemed like a theory a researcher might reasonably advance. I have no problem getting rid of it if we decide it doesn't fit.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is one of those SCPs that handily makes up for a lack of creepy by generating a sense of wonder. Upvoted.

Now, down to brass tacks. Given how hard these lifeforms are to recapture or destroy if they escape containment, would this qualify for a Euclid rating? Also, it might be interesting to see the Founation intentionally allow some of them into a sample of concrete, then perform tests on the fossils and/or the concrete. How does having these things inside it affect the strength of a stone or concrete? If their presence weakens it, then these things pose a credible threat to a lot of structures if they ever become widespread. How finely-pulverized are disposed-of materials? A grain of sand is significantly larger than a microbe, which means there could be fossilized plankton swimming around all over the place.

This is cool enough conceptually for an upvote, though I'm left wondering about a few things.

How exactly are these creatures being observed? They might be able to move through stone as if it was water, but light certainly can't. We'd only be able to directly observe objects that are touching the surface(s) of the stone, unless some sort of sonic imaging is in use.

Also, I'd ditch the suggestion that these are "organisms that adapted to life in solid rock", it sounds a bit silly.
